02.r: To make a fellow Israelite pay interest on a loan.
02.n: The verb from which the noun 'interest' comes, in its causative form: the brief's lexicon gives 'to make to give interest'. Gesenius gives the first sense as TO BITE, as a serpent, then metaphorically to vex, to oppress, and to lend on usury, citing Deut. 23:20 (this verse in the Hebrew numbering, evidently, since the English numbers it one lower). He adds that receiving interest was thought to mark a sordid person and an oppressor of the weak.

03.r: A fellow Israelite, counted as family.
03.n: The brief's lexicon lists brother of the same parents, relative, and one of the same tribe; STEPBible's gloss here is 'countryman'.

04.r: The first of three kinds of interest the law names.
04.n: Literally 'interest of silver': the noun is joined to the next word. The verse repeats the noun three times, so that no kind of loan is left out.

05.n: Gesenius gives the first sense as silver, so called from its pale colour; our English keeps 'silver' throughout.

06.r: The second kind: interest on food lent.

07.r: Food lent, to be repaid with more.
07.n: Gesenius gives first an eating, then food, especially corn, grain, provision.

08.r: The third kind, covering everything else.

10.r: Anything at all that might be lent.
10.n: The word's first senses are word and speech, but it is also the ordinary word for a thing or matter. The ASV and YLT fold it into 'anything'.

12.r: Anything on which interest could be charged.
12.n: The same verb as at the start of the verse, now in its plain form, which the brief's lexicon gives as 'to give interest'. With 'thing' as its subject it reads 'that yields interest'; it can also be taken impersonally, 'on which one pays interest'. Most translations make it passive, 'that is lent upon usury'.

_extra.7: καὶ (and): added by the Greek translators between the kinds of interest.
_extra.10: καὶ (and): added again before the third kind.

02.n: ἐκτοκίζω, to lend at interest, built on τόκος, interest.

04.n: τόκος, interest; the Greek repeats it three times, as the Hebrew does.

12.n: ἐκδανείζω, to lend out. The Greek changes the person: 'whatever you lend', where the Hebrew has 'that bears interest'.
